analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax credits, health savings accounts, and drug importation.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one House member with no cosponsors, was referred to eight committees and a subcommittee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the 2010 health care law (the ACA) and its companion reconciliation act outright, then replaced them with a set of tax-based provisions: a refundable tax credit for insurance premiums plus health savings account contributions, larger HSA deductions without a high-deductible plan requirement, letting up to $500 in unused flexible spending account money roll over, full deduction of medical expenses, and tax credits for insurance against bad surgical outcomes. It also would let people buy health insurance across state lines and let anyone import FDA-approved prescription drugs, including insulin, that meet US safety requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own insurance would get a refundable credit covering premiums plus HSA contributions, and consumers could import FDA-approved drugs from abroad, potentially lowering prices. Higher-income taxpayers gain the most from the expanded HSA deductions (up to $8,000 per person, $16,000 per couple) and the removal of the 7.5% income threshold on medical expense deductions, which only matter to people who itemize or owe income tax.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces ACA premium subsidies with a refundable tax credit covering health insurance premiums plus health savings account contributions, capped at a taxpayer's income and payroll taxes [S2].
Lets individuals buy health insurance from issuers in any state, as long as the issuer complies with its home state's laws [S3].
Repeals federal restrictions on importing prescription drugs, allowing people to import FDA-approved drugs, including insulin, with a 60-day review deadline [S2, S3].

Expands health savings accounts: larger deductions ($8,000 individual, $16,000 joint, indexed to inflation) and no requirement to hold a high-deductible health plan, and permits using HSAs for Medigap and high-deductible premiums [S3].

Lets up to $500 of unused flexible spending account health benefits carry over to the next year or be paid back to the employee, and removes the 7.5%-of-income threshold so all medical expenses are deductible [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who gained coverage or protections under the ACA would lose them immediately on repeal: the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions, premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, dependent coverage, and the guarantee of essential benefits. The replacement tax benefits are worth little to people with no income tax or payroll tax liability, so lower-income households would bear the largest loss. Insurers and providers would lose the ACA's mandate-driven customer base and new regulations.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who gained coverage under the ACA

drawbacks.text: Full repeal of the ACA, effective as if it had never been enacted, would strip away guaranteed issue for pre-existing conditions, premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and dependent coverage that had just taken effect [S2].

The replacement benefits run through the tax code: refundable credits are capped at income and payroll taxes paid, and HSA deductions and the medical-expense deduction change are worth the most to people with higher incomes and tax liabilities, so the relief is unevenly distributed [S3].

Buying insurance across state lines lets policies follow the rules of whichever state the insurer chooses, which could let plans avoid consumer protections in the buyer's home state; the bill imposes no minimum benefit standards of its own [S3].

The bill creates a new tax-favored market for 'negative outcomes insurance' covering surgical harms and excludes malpractice arbitration awards from income tax, shifting malpractice disputes away from courts toward a private insurance and arbitration system with no track record [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs genuinely consumer-friendly provisions — drug importation and HSA/FSA flexibility — with a complete repeal of the ACA before its replacement was in place, which would have taken existing protections and subsidies away from millions of lower-income Americans while offering tax-code benefits that mostly reach people who already owe taxes or itemize. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the poorest households, who gained the most from the ACA, would lose the most under this swap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single member with no cosponsors, referred to eight House committees and then a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without ever getting a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the Private Option Health Care Act on May 27, 2010 [S1].
It was referred to eight House committees: Energy and Commerce, Appropriations, House Administration, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Natural Resources, Judiciary, and Rules [S5].
On June 29, 2010, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was recorded [S5].
No committee reported the bill and no vote was ever taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the ACA remained fully in effect, which preserved its coverage expansions, subsidies, and protections for people who had just gained coverage. The health industries whose businesses the ACA had reshaped, including insurers operating under its rules, also kept the status quo rather than facing sudden repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1, S5].

against.name: House committee chairs, 111th Congress
against.role: Chairs of the eight committees the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it moved only to a subcommittee and died there [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan alignment on the merits can be measured from the record.

industries.note: Repealing the ACA would end the individual mandate that delivers customers to insurers but also end the guaranteed-issue and benefit rules that constrain them; buying insurance across state lines would increase competition while letting plans escape state consumer protections.
The bill repeals restrictions on importing FDA-approved prescription drugs, which would expose US prices to competition from cheaper drugs sold abroad.

industries.industry: Financial services firms offering health savings accounts
industries.note: The bill greatly expands HSA eligibility and limits (up to $8,000/$16,000) without a high-deductible plan requirement, enlarging the pool of tax-advantaged assets these firms manage, with the largest benefits going to higher-income savers.

industries.industry: Physicians and medical providers facing malpractice claims
industries.note: Tax-free binding arbitration awards and a new 'negative outcomes insurance' market would shift malpractice disputes away from jury verdicts, a change providers and their insurers have long sought.
